title: 2  Preface
text:
Just matter of what was libido for Freud, this is my little contribution to a topic that I am very passionate about.
These notes are my attempt to truly understand how VAR models work, going into the details to see how the mechanisms behind them operate, with simple examples that make each step clear. Most of the material is based on lectures by Professor Roberto Golinelli, the Macroeconometric Forecasting (MFx) course by the IMF, and Stock, J. H., & Watson, M. W. (2001).
They may be useful if you already have a basic knowledge of time series analysis, and more specifically of AR models.

section: 3.2 Why is VAR simple and flexible, so useful and used?
text:
3.2 Why is VAR simple and flexible, so useful and used?
A standard AR or ARDL model4 is inherently unidirectional: the researcher must decide, a priori, which variable belongs on the left-hand side and which on the right. But the true data-generating process (DGP) is always unobservable, we can never verify whether the relationship we impose reflects reality, or is simply a convenient assumption.
VARs sidestep this problem by allowing for simultaneity, avoiding the constraint of unidirectionality. As shown above every variable can affect, and be affected by, every other variable, with no need to decide in advance who is endogenous and who is exogenous. Since every equation shares the same regressors (lags of all variables) each can be estimated independently via OLS.
Also because in microeconomics, this chicken-and-egg problem can sometimes be resolved through natural temporal ordering: education precedes wages, so treating it as exogenous is defensible. In macroeconomics, this precedence rarely exists, following the previous example: GDP and inflation are determined simultaneously, within the same period.
This is what makes the VAR both simpler and more flexible: it is essentially atheoretical in structure, treating every variable as potentially endogenous and letting the data reveal the dynamics, rather than imposing a priori who (exogenous) influences whom (endogenous).

title: 3  VAR intro
text:
3.3 VAR from a mathematical POV
A VAR is an \(n\)-equation, \(n\)-variable linear model in which each variable is in turn explained by its own lagged values, plus current and past values of the remaining \(n-1\) variables.
Example:
The easiest case is a VAR(1), where the number inside parenthesis indicates the number of lags, with just two variable \(x_t\) and \(y_t\).
It could be expressed in equation-by-equation form:
\[
\begin{aligned}
x_t &= c_1 + \phi_{11}\, x_{t-1} + \phi_{12}\, y_{t-1} + w_{1t} \\
y_t &= c_2 + \phi_{21}\, x_{t-1} + \phi_{22}\, y_{t-1} + w_{2t}
\end{aligned}
\tag{3.1}\]
Or in matrix form:
\[
Z_t = c + \Phi\, Z_{t-1} + w_t
\tag{3.2}\]
Where:
\[
Z_t = \begin{bmatrix} x_t \\ y_t \end{bmatrix}, \qquad
\Phi = \begin{bmatrix} \phi_{11} & \phi_{12} \\ \phi_{21} & \phi_{22} \end{bmatrix}, \qquad
w_t = \begin{bmatrix} w_{1t} \\ w_{2t} \end{bmatrix}
\tag{3.3}\]
It is easy to verify that Equation 3.2 is equivalent to Equation 3.1 by expanding the matrix product:
\[
\Phi Z_{t-1} = \begin{bmatrix} \phi_{11} & \phi_{12} \\ \phi_{21} & \phi_{22} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} x_{t-1} \\ y_{t-1} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \phi_{11} x_{t-1} + \phi_{12} y_{t-1} \\ \phi_{21} x_{t-1} + \phi_{22} y_{t-1} \end{bmatrix}
\tag{3.4}\]

title: 3  VAR intro
section: 3.4 How VAR is used in macroeconometrics?
text:
3.4 How VAR is used in macroeconometrics?
VAR offers a coherent and credible framework for four distinct tasks: data description, forecasting, structural inference and policy analysis.
For forecasting and data description, a reduced-form VAR is sufficient: forecasting only requires the conditional mean of future values given the past, with no need to take a stance on the underlying structural relationships among the variables.
For structural inference and policy analysis, however, the reduced-form VAR is not enough — these tasks require an identified VAR5. In this context, the goal is to analyze the impact of structural shocks. This is done with impulse-response analysis6 and with forecast error variance decomposition7.

title: 3  VAR intro
text:
Multivariate: VAR models several variables jointly, not just one. Each variable depends on its own lags and on the lags of all other variables in the system. (Univariate AR: only own past values. VAR: own past + others’ past.)↩︎
Joint dynamics: All variables move together and influence each other over time — not “multiple” series side by side.↩︎
Endogenous vs. exogenous: an endogenous variable is determined within the system, the model explains it, and it can be both cause and effect of the others. An exogenous variable is taken as given from outside the system, it may influence the endogenous variables but is never explained by them.↩︎
ARDL (AutoRegressive Distributed Lag): a single-equation model in which a dependent variable is explained by its own lags (the autoregressive part) plus current and past values of one or more explanatory variables (the distributed-lag part). For a single regressor:
\[
y_t = c + \sum_{i=1}^{p} \phi_i\, y_{t-i} + \sum_{j=0}^{q} \beta_j\, x_{t-j} + \varepsilon_t
\]↩︎
Identified VAR: identification means separating correlation from causation — the reduced-form residuals are correlated across equations, but correlation alone cannot tell us which shock caused what. Two main ways to identify a VAR, and so to identify shocks’ effects:

Recursive ordering: impose a causal chain among variables (via Cholesky decomposition), assuming variable 1 affects all others within the period, variable 2 affects all but variable 1, and so on.
Structural approach: impose restrictions derived from economic theory instead of an arbitrary ordering.

↩︎
Impulse-response function (IRF): Traces the effect of a one-time shock to one variable on the current and future values of all variables in the system, holding everything else constant. It answers: “if variable X is hit by a shock today, how does variable Y react today, next period, two periods ahead, …?”↩︎
Forecast error variance decomposition (FEVD): At each forecast horizon, splits the forecast error variance of a variable into the share explained by shocks to itself versus shocks to each of the other variables. It answers: “how much of the uncertainty in forecasting X comes from X’s own shocks, and how much from shocks to the other variables?”↩︎

title: 4  From AR to VAR
text:
5 From AR to VAR
Three ideas — recursive substitution, the dynamic multiplier, and the Wold (moving-average) representation — are usually taught as separate topics. They are not: they are three views of a single question, how does a shock propagate through time? We answer it first in the scalar AR(1) world, where every step is transparent, and then replay the same argument in the matrix VAR world, where the algebra is heavier but the logic is identical. The reward is a clean bridge: the moving-average weights are the dynamic multipliers are the impulse responses.
The route is the same on both sides:
We walk this route once for the AR(1) (Part A), then once for the VAR (Part B).

title: 4  From AR to VAR
section: 5.1 Part A — The scalar case: AR(1)
text:
5.1 Part A — The scalar case: AR(1)

5.1.1 Recursive substitution
Take a first-order autoregression (the constant is dropped without loss — it only shifts the mean), with \(w_t\) a white-noise shock:
\[
y_t = \phi\, y_{t-1} + w_t,
\qquad w_t \sim \text{WN}(0,\sigma^2)
\tag{5.1}\]
Given a starting value \(y_{-1}\) and the sequence of shocks \(w_0, w_1, \dots\), the equation holds at every date. Substituting each value into the next:
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_0 &= \phi\, y_{-1} + w_0 \\
y_1 &= \phi\, y_0 + w_1 = \phi^{2} y_{-1} + \phi\, w_0 + w_1 \\
y_2 &= \phi\, y_1 + w_2 = \phi^{3} y_{-1} + \phi^{2} w_0 + \phi\, w_1 + w_2
\end{aligned}
\tag{5.2}\]
Continuing to date \(t\) gives the general solution:
\[
y_t = \phi^{\,t+1} y_{-1} + \sum_{i=0}^{t} \phi^{\,i}\, w_{t-i}
= \phi^{\,t+1} y_{-1} + w_t + \phi\, w_{t-1} + \cdots + \phi^{\,t} w_0
\tag{5.3}\]
The value of \(y_t\) splits into two pieces: a transient \(\phi^{\,t+1} y_{-1}\) carried by the initial condition, and a weighted sum of every shock since the start, with weight \(\phi^{\,i}\) on the shock \(i\) periods ago.


5.1.2 The dynamic multiplier = the impulse response
Because Equation 5.3 writes \(y_t\) as a linear function of the shocks, the effect of a single shock is read off directly. Restarting the count at an arbitrary date \(t\):
\[
y_{t+j} = \phi^{\,j+1} y_{t-1} + \sum_{i=0}^{j}\phi^{\,i}\, w_{t+j-i}
\tag{5.4}\]
and differentiating with respect to the shock \(w_t\):
\[
\frac{\partial\, y_{t+j}}{\partial\, w_t} = \phi^{\,j}
\tag{5.5}\]
This quantity — the dynamic multiplier — is the response of \(y\), \(j\) periods ahead, to a one-unit shock today. Two features matter. First, it depends only on the horizon \(j\), not on the date \(t\): the system reacts to a shock the same way no matter when it lands. Second, this is exactly an impulse-response function — trace \(\phi^{\,j}\) for \(j = 0, 1, 2, \dots\) and you have drawn the system’s response to an impulse.
The shape depends entirely on \(\phi\):

\(0<\phi<1\): monotone geometric decay toward zero;
\(-1<\phi<0\): decay with alternating sign (damped oscillation);
\(\phi>1\): explosive monotone growth;
\(\phi<-1\): explosive oscillation.

The dividing line is \(|\phi|<1\): inside it a shock’s effect eventually dies out and the system is stable; outside it the effect grows without bound. The borderline \(\phi=1\) is the random walk, where \(\phi^{\,j}=1\) for every \(j\) and a shock’s effect is permanent.
Move the slider through all four regimes — this is the response \(\partial y_{t+j}/\partial w_t = \phi^{\,j}\):

viewof phi = Inputs.range([-1.2, 1.2], {value: 0.8, step: 0.05, label: "phi"})







{
  const H = 20;
  const data = d3.range(0, H + 1).map(j => ({j, resp: Math.pow(phi, j)}));
  return Plot.plot({
    height: 300,
    marginLeft: 55,
    x: { label: "horizon j" },
    y: { label: "response = phi^j", grid: true },
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleY([0]),
      Plot.barY(data, { x: "j", y: "resp",
        fill: d => d.resp >= 0 ? "#4c78a8" : "#e45756" })
    ]
  });
}








5.1.3 From recursive substitution to the Wold representation
Now let the process have been running not from date \(-1\) but from the infinite past — equivalently, let \(t\to\infty\) in Equation 5.3. When \(|\phi|<1\) the transient vanishes, \(\phi^{\,t+1} y_{-1}\to 0\), and only the shock sum survives:
\[
y_t = \sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\phi^{\,i}\, w_{t-i}
= w_t + \phi\, w_{t-1} + \phi^{2} w_{t-2} + \cdots
\tag{5.6}\]
This is the MA(\(\infty\)), or Wold, representation: the current value \(y_t\) as a weighted sum of all past shocks. It is nothing more than recursive substitution pushed to its limit under stationarity — and its weights \(\phi^{\,i}\) are exactly the dynamic multipliers of Equation 5.5.
The same object is reached algebraically with the lag operator \(L\) (with \(L\,w_t = w_{t-1}\)): writing Equation 5.1 as \((1-\phi L)\,y_t = w_t\) and inverting,1
\[
y_t = \frac{w_t}{1-\phi L}
= \Big(\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\phi^{\,i} L^{i}\Big) w_t,
\tag{5.7}\]
which reproduces Equation 5.6 term by term. The geometric series converges for exactly the reason the transient dies: \(|\phi|<1\).

title: 4  From AR to VAR
section: 5.2 Part B — The matrix case: VAR(p)
text:
5.2 Part B — The matrix case: VAR(p)
Everything above now repeats with one substitution: scalars become matrices. Nothing in the logic changes.

5.2.1 Recursive substitution for the VAR
The reduced-form VAR(1) (again dropping the constant) is the matrix twin of Equation 5.1, with \(Z_t\) stacking the \(n\) variables, \(\Phi\) an \(n\times n\) coefficient matrix, and \(w_t\) the vector of innovations:
\[
Z_t = \Phi\, Z_{t-1} + w_t
\tag{5.8}\]
Substituting exactly as before — every \(\phi^{\,i}\) becoming \(\Phi^{\,i}\):
\[
Z_t = \Phi^{\,t+1} Z_{-1} + \sum_{i=0}^{t}\Phi^{\,i}\, w_{t-i}
\tag{5.9}\]
Same structure as Equation 5.3: a transient \(\Phi^{\,t+1} Z_{-1}\) plus a weighted sum of past shock vectors, now with matrix weights \(\Phi^{\,i}\).


5.2.2 The VMA(\(\infty\)): the multivariate Wold representation
Letting the process run from the infinite past, if the VAR is stationary the transient dies, \(\Phi^{\,t+1} Z_{-1}\to 0\),2 and
\[
Z_t = \sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\Phi^{\,i}\, w_{t-i}
= \sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\Psi_i\, w_{t-i},
\qquad \Psi_i = \Phi^{\,i},\;\; \Psi_0 = I_n
\tag{5.10}\]
This is the VMA(\(\infty\)), the multivariate Wold representation. For a VAR(1) the moving-average matrices are simply the powers \(\Psi_i=\Phi^{\,i}\) — the literal analogue of the scalar \(\phi^{\,i}\). For a general VAR(\(p\)) the same object is obtained with the lag operator: writing the model as \(G(L)\,Z_t = w_t\) and inverting the matrix polynomial,
\[
Z_t = \mu + G(L)^{-1} w_t = \mu + \sum_{i=0}^{\infty}\Psi_i\, w_{t-i},
\tag{5.11}\]
where the \(\Psi_i\) are the coefficient matrices of the power series \(G(L)^{-1}=\sum_i \Psi_i L^{i}\) (with \(\Psi_0=I_n\)), and \(\mu\) is the mean, restored once the constant is put back.
The parallel with the scalar case is one-to-one:









AR(1) — scalar
VAR(p) — matrix

\(y_t=\phi\, y_{t-1}+w_t\)
\(Z_t=\Phi\, Z_{t-1}+w_t\)

\(y_t=\phi^{\,t+1}y_{-1}+\sum_i \phi^{\,i} w_{t-i}\)
\(Z_t=\Phi^{\,t+1}Z_{-1}+\sum_i \Phi^{\,i} w_{t-i}\)

\(\Psi_i\;\;(=\Phi^{\,i}\text{ if }p=1)\)


representation
MA(\(\infty\))
VMA(\(\infty\))


stationarity
\(\lvert\phi\rvert<1\)
roots of \(\det G(L)=0\) outside the unit circle


multiplier \(=\) IRF
\(\partial y_{t+j}/\partial w_t=\phi^{\,j}\)
\(\partial Z_{t+j}/\partial w_t'=\Psi_j\)





5.2.3 The multiplier becomes the impulse response
Differentiating Equation 5.11 with respect to the shock vector, exactly as in the scalar case:
\[
\frac{\partial\, Z_{t+j}}{\partial\, w_t'} = \Psi_j
\tag{5.12}\]
Each matrix \(\Psi_j\) is the system’s response, \(j\) periods ahead, to a one-unit impulse in the shocks: its \((k,\ell)\) entry is the reaction of variable \(k\) to a shock in variable \(\ell\). Where the scalar multiplier \(\phi^{\,j}\) traced a single decaying (or oscillating, or explosive) path, \(\Psi_j\) now carries both own- and cross-effects, so responses can travel between variables, oscillate, and feed back through the system before dying out — the feedback loop of the previous chapter, made quantitative.
For a bivariate VAR(1) this is a \(2\times2\) grid: each variable’s reaction to each shock. The sliders are the four entries of \(\Phi\); each panel traces an entry of \(\Psi_j=\Phi^{\,j}\) over the horizon \(j\):

viewof phi11 = Inputs.range([-0.95, 0.95], {value: 0.5, step: 0.05, label: "Phi 1,1 (x on own lag)"})







viewof phi12 = Inputs.range([-0.95, 0.95], {value: 0.3, step: 0.05, label: "Phi 1,2 (x on lagged y)"})







viewof phi21 = Inputs.range([-0.95, 0.95], {value: 0.2, step: 0.05, label: "Phi 2,1 (y on lagged x)"})







viewof phi22 = Inputs.range([-0.95, 0.95], {value: 0.5, step: 0.05, label: "Phi 2,2 (y on own lag)"})







{
  const H = 20;
  const Phi = [[phi11, phi12], [phi21, phi22]];
  const mul = (A, B) => [
    [A[0][0]*B[0][0] + A[0][1]*B[1][0], A[0][0]*B[0][1] + A[0][1]*B[1][1]],
    [A[1][0]*B[0][0] + A[1][1]*B[1][0], A[1][0]*B[0][1] + A[1][1]*B[1][1]]
  ];
  const vars = ["x", "y"];
  let Psi = [[1, 0], [0, 1]];
  const rows = [];
  for (let j = 0; j <= H; j++) {
    for (let k = 0; k < 2; k++) {
      for (let l = 0; l < 2; l++) {
        rows.push({
          j,
          resp: Psi[k][l],
          respVar: "response of " + vars[k],
          shockVar: "shock to " + vars[l]
        });
      }
    }
    Psi = mul(Phi, Psi);
  }
  return Plot.plot({
    height: 380,
    marginLeft: 55,
    x: { label: "horizon j" },
    y: { label: "response", grid: true },
    fx: { label: null },
    fy: { label: null },
    marks: [
      Plot.ruleY([0]),
      Plot.barY(rows, {
        x: "j",
        y: "resp",
        fx: "shockVar",
        fy: "respVar",
        fill: d => d.resp >= 0 ? "#4c78a8" : "#e45756"
      })
    ]
  });
}






Try pushing the coefficients up: some combinations put a root of \(\det G(L)\) inside the unit circle and the responses explode instead of dying out — nonstationarity, made visible.


5.2.4 Where this leads
These \(\Psi_j\) are the reduced-form impulse responses: they answer “what happens if the reduced-form innovation \(w_{\ell t}\) moves by one unit?” But the innovations are correlated across equations, so a shock to one variable rarely arrives in isolation — which makes the reduced-form responses hard to read as clean economic experiments. Recovering structural impulse responses, where the shocks are mutually uncorrelated and interpretable, requires identifying the VAR — orthogonalizing the innovations. That is the subject of the next chapter, together with the forecast error variance decomposition, which uses these very same \(\Psi_j\) to split forecast uncertainty across shocks.

title: 4  From AR to VAR
text:
The inversion of \((1-\phi L)\) in Equation 5.7 is a geometric series \(\sum_i \phi^{i} L^{i}\) that converges only when \(|\phi| < 1\). If \(|\phi| \ge 1\) the weights do not decay, the sum of past shocks diverges, and no stable MA(\(\infty\)) exists — the process is nonstationary (the random walk \(\phi = 1\) is the borderline case).
For the VAR the requirement is the same in spirit but heavier to state: \(G(L)^{-1}\) exists as a convergent power series only if \(G(L)\) is invertible, which holds if and only if all \(np\) roots of
\[\det\!\left(I_n - G_1 L - G_2 L^{2} - \cdots - G_p L^{p}\right) = 0\]
lie outside the unit circle — equivalently, the inverse roots (the eigenvalues of the companion matrix) lie inside it. It is the exact matrix generalization of \(|\phi| < 1\): one condition on a single scalar becomes a condition on the modulus of every root of a matrix polynomial.↩︎
The inversion of \((1-\phi L)\) in Equation 5.7 is a geometric series \(\sum_i \phi^{i} L^{i}\) that converges only when \(|\phi| < 1\). If \(|\phi| \ge 1\) the weights do not decay, the sum of past shocks diverges, and no stable MA(\(\infty\)) exists — the process is nonstationary (the random walk \(\phi = 1\) is the borderline case).
For the VAR the requirement is the same in spirit but heavier to state: \(G(L)^{-1}\) exists as a convergent power series only if \(G(L)\) is invertible, which holds if and only if all \(np\) roots of
\[\det\!\left(I_n - G_1 L - G_2 L^{2} - \cdots - G_p L^{p}\right) = 0\]
